entries.title: Inside the Play That Made the Commanders' Tyler Owens Go Viral
entries.summary: His extra efforts on a punt return wowed the internet, but teammates and coaches were even more impressed.
entries.content:
J.J. Watt called it “legitimately one of the greatest football plays I've ever seen.” Tom Brady sang its praises on national TV. Michael Irvin labeled it an “insane effort” that should lead to more playing time.

Commanders safety Tyler Owens went viral this week for the one type of football play that very rarely garners attention, let alone internet fame: a special teams rep. But when you see a player fight his way through a double-team, plow over said double-team and deliver a Goldberg-esque spear — all within about 10 seconds — no superlative seems hyperbolic.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2099248175085498563But what was it like on the field? The Washington Sun spoke with Owens, his teammates and coaches about what happened in real time.

In the second quarter of Sunday’s game against the Eagles, Owens — one of two gunners, along with Percy Butler — lines up on the right side of the field for a punt. Two Eagles jammers, Darius Cooper and Jonathan Jones, line up directly across from him. 

Punter Tress Way: Before every punt, I look out there and I see who's on Percy and I see who's on [Owens]. And whenever I see T.O. doubled, the first thing that goes in my head for those guys on the other side of the ball is, “good luck.”

Special teams coordinator Larry Izzo: I saw he was doubled early. I saw him split it, and then my eyes kind of went back deeper down the field to where the ball was.

Head coach Dan Quinn: I didn't see the start of it on the field. Might have caught the corner where he beat the [double team] to go down the field

Cooper and Jones cocoon Owens for 10 yards, not allowing him to break free up the field, but Owens continues to charge forward. 

Owens: The first three punts I was backside, so I was inside releasing. They had caught on. The [punt] before they were holding me bad — they had to jump on me. They already knew where I was going, so on that [play] I tried to give them something different, and they still played it good, so I just had to fight through it.

Izzo: John Glenn, coach of the gunners, does a great job with our guys every week of working the tools. All the different releases, whether it's an outside release, inside release, stretch, split. So there's a lot that goes into it, a lot of practice time that led to that play. But what you saw there was just a sheer will not to be blocked.

While holding off Jones with his right arm, Owens stiff-arms Cooper to the ground. He then steps over Cooper, gets pushed from behind by Eagles linebacker Jeremiah Trotter Jr. and stiff-arms Jones into the ground as well — all while maintaining his balance. Meanwhile, Eagles return man Britain Covey fields the punt. 

Butler: I just ran down, and the returner came inside off of me. So I knew he was going into the net [of Commanders defenders]. So I'm like, “Shit, he finna get fucked up.”

Longsnapper Tyler Ott: Normally, I'm not one of the first ones down there in coverage, but just tried to make sure that the returner had to go back into the middle of the field.

Safety Jeremy Reaves: I'm controlling the middle, and I got [Covey] to turn back, stop his feet.

Owens: I was trying to keep as much space off of me as I could.

As Covey is funneled toward the middle of the field, he runs straight into a charging Owens, who is flanked by Reaves and linebacker Jordan Magee. Covey jumps in the air and is speared backward by Owens, with Magee coming over the top to finish him off.

Way: I saw him knock that second to last guy down, and then when I saw Covey make that cut, and T.O. was right there, I was like, “Here we go.”

Linebacker Kain Medrano: When I saw Tyler, I knew [Covey] was going to get put on his back.

Tight end Ben Sinnott: I had a crazy angle right in front of me. And I'm like, “OK I might be able to make a tackle here,” and then [Owens] comes up and smokes him.

Tight end Colson Yankoff: I just saw bodies flying, and then smacking the dude. It was awesome. It was phenomenal.

Reaves: When he jumped, I knew somebody was gonna be there. I ain't know who, but I had a feeling it was gonna be [Owens] or [Butler].

Owens: I see him running towards me, and I'm getting ready to fit him up. And then [Reaves] is flying in, and then Jordan funneling in. So he didn't really have nowhere to go. So I just put my shoulder on him.

Ott: I ended up on the ground. I turned back, and I got to see the aftermath of basically a suplex.

Butler: It reminded me of the Nick Bellore play from last year when we played the Giants. I just seen him wrap him up and kind of like [the WWE finishing move] RKO — because I was finna go get in on it from the back, but I was like, “Nah, let me let him finish him off.” I was just hyped for my boy.

Linebacker Leo Chenal: I was late down there. I didn't see it, to be honest, but I saw a bunch of guys just getting excited. I knew with T.O. in the area it's probably T.O.

Whether they saw it in the moment or watched it later on replay, players and coaches knew the play was special. 

Yankoff: He's a dude that we rely on heavily on those units and that's why. He's a dog, he's a freak athlete.

Chenal: I agree with the sentiment that it's one of the best special teams plays I've ever seen. You pull two guys as a gunner, and then going down there, perfect form tackle. Doesn't get better than that.

Quinn: And it was so him, like, “Oh, thanks, man. That's what I do.” Like it was like no big deal. And you're like, “Man, this is a really big deal.” It was a really cool play and I got to see it probably like everybody else did from the network feed afterwards. And it was one of my favorite plays in a long time on special teams for sure.

Izzo: This is my 30th year in the NFL. I have to say, it was probably the most impressive play on special teams that I've seen, to my memory. This was just a complete ass-whooping.

entries.title: Border Wall Construction Is Beginning in Texas' Big Bend Region
entries.summary: Customs and Border Protection said “border wall panel installation is underway” in Hudspeth County.
entries.content:
By Rebecca Santana

COMSTOCK, Texas — The Trump administration has started building the border wall through a west Texas section of the Big Bend region, marking the first major construction in an area of the U.S.-Mexico border where the administration's plans have met with heavy opposition.

The start of construction marks an important milestone in the administration's $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology as it seeks to make good on a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump to finish the wall. And it comes as Customs and Border Protection says it has doubled the pace at which it is building the wall across the U.S.-Mexico border.

Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1. There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.

The agency did not say when the panels had been installed. On a map on the agency’s website where it posts updates of wall construction across the entire southern border, a photo showed a crane lifting one of the 30-foot tall steel wall panels into place while construction workers looked on.

The new activity was separate from a border infrastructure project in the nearby Big Bend National Park, where the administration has temporarily suspended construction in an attempt at outreach to opponents.

In the broader Big Bend region of Texas, CBP has run up against concerted opposition from landowners, environmental groups, business owners and ranchers who say the remote region isn't a high traffic area for illegal immigration.

Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.

Clara Benson, one of the founders of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition which has been fighting against CBP’s plans, said in an interview Friday that the organization had been receiving reports of trucks moving supplies into the remote area along the Rio Grande and that contractors had been clearing yards to stage supplies.

But speaking from Washington, D.C. where she and others in the coalition were meeting with lawmakers, she said that the organization and others would continue to fight the wall-building plans across the region.

“We will continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is. We will continue fighting to the end,” said Benson. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”

The news comes as the administration is speeding forward with a plan to line the entire border with a combination of 30-foot tall steel bollard walls, barriers designed to stop vehicles from crossing the border, new patrol roads and various technologies to deter and detect migrants or smugglers from crossing the border.

Customs and Border Protection said that they are building an average of 12 miles of barriers a week across the 2,000-mile border with Mexico and recently hit a milestone of 200 miles of new barriers built since the second Trump administration took office.

The 12-miles a week average is double the pace that the agency's head, Rodney Scott, cited earlier this year.

The agency has faced opposition from environmental groups, a small town that worries the wall will cause flooding in its area, Native Americans who say the construction is disturbing sacred sites and landowners who say the construction will infringe on their land.

In Texas much of the opposition has centered on the agency's plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state's southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world. But up and down river outside the park, much of the land is owned by private landowners, many of whom have pushed back against the government's efforts.

Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.

Activists and landowners have also shown up at county meetings to push their elected officials not to cooperate with contractors hired by CBP to build the wall, and many landowners have refused to allow government officials or contractors onto their land to survey it.

entries.title: Trump Calling MAGA Inc. Funds ‘My Money’ Spurs FEC Complaint
entries.summary: Federal law bars officeholders from soliciting, directing or spending super PAC funds.
entries.content:
In early September, President Donald Trump told reporters that his super PAC, MAGA Inc., had close to $1 billion — which he described as “my money.”

A campaign finance watchdog says that statement, among others Trump has made in the past few months asserting personal control of the super PAC, violated federal law, according to a new complaint filed with the Federal Election Commission this week.

Federal officeholders are prohibited from soliciting, directing or spending funds controlled by outside groups like MAGA Inc., which can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money. The Campaign Legal Center pointed to Trump’s previous comments in their filing, as well as private and public meetings involving PAC spending and fundraising efforts.

“Trump’s public statements are thus a remarkable admission of a serious campaign finance violation,” Campaign Legal Center wrote in the complaint, which was first reported by The New York Times.

MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer called the complaint “frivolous” in a statement to The Washington Sun and dismissed Campaign Legal Center’s “smears” against the Trump administration.

“MAGA Inc. fully complies with the law,” Pfeiffer said.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment .

Trump has repeatedly staked his claim to control of the super PAC’s funds. In addition to his Oval Office comments Sept. 4, the president corrected Punchbowl News’ Jake Sherman in August when Sherman characterized MAGA Inc. as being controlled by Trump’s allies during a sit-down interview.

“Not my allies, I control it,” the president interjected.

A couple weeks after that, on Aug. 21, Trump told reporters before boarding Air Force One that he would pour “a lot” of MAGA Inc. money into the midterms.

“I’ll be spending a lot of that money for — and my own money — but I’ll be spending a lot

of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates,” Trump said.

The FEC does not have enough commissioners to conduct an investigation or otherwise act on the complaint.

While Trump nominated two Republicans in February, a Senate committee has not scheduled a hearing to advance the commissioner candidates — and it is unlikely to do so before the 2026 election.

entries.title: Spanberger Pushes New Data Center Guardrails in Virginia
entries.summary: The Virginia governor signed an executive order to increase oversight of the state’s data centers.
entries.content:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday implementing a “data center accountability framework” after urging by conservation groups that have been fighting for greater oversight of data centers in the state.

The executive order would ban the use of non-disclosure agreements that have made it harder for the public to follow proposed data center development. The order would also expedite development of data center noise regulations and direct a review of diesel and other backup generators used to power data centers.

Much of the plan requires approval by the Virginia General Assembly, which won’t convene again until January. But Spanberger told reporters at a news conference Friday that “the state has to show leadership”

“We are in a place where day by day community members are demanding action,” said Spanberger, who was joined by representatives from conservation groups. “As localities continue to have the option of choosing to reject or accept applications for data centers to come into their communities, it’s vital that the state actually provide a framework for them to be able to make those thoughtful decisions.”

Data centers have been in Virginia for decades. Loudoun, Prince William and Fairfax counties — a region now known as “Data Center Alley” — are home to more than 300 data centers. Virginia is one of several states that offers a sales and use tax exemption for data center equipment, including servers, mainframes, cabling, HVAC systems and water storage tanks.

But this spring, souring public sentiment spurred some legislators to try to take away the tax exemption, which saved Virginia data centers $1.9 billion last year. While they ultimately weren’t successful in repealing the exemption, Spanberger signed into law a first-of-its-kind tax on data center energy consumption.

There’s also been change at the local level.

On Tuesday, the Board of Supervisors in Loudoun County, which has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, voted to advance a resolution pausing new data center development for 12 months.

And in early July, Blackstone’s QTS abandoned plans to build a massive data center campus on the edge of Manassas National Battlefield Park, a historic Civil War battle site. Bloomberg first reported the developer had walked away from the project, which had been ensnared in a yearslong legal battle.

Data center developers and operators, as well as the labor unions that see the projects as incredible opportunities for their members, have been doing damage control amid the backlash.

Virginia Connects, the state arm of the Data Center Coalition, a data center industry group, spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads this spring trying to turn around public perception, to no avail.

The Data Center Coalition did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Connor Kish, director of the Sierra Club’s Virginia chapter, told reporters that creating a framework is “critical” for addressing backlash from communities that have expressed frustration with noise pollution and environmental impacts, data centers’ impact on electricity prices and a lack of transparency into new data center development.

“The world's largest corporations are capable of doing better, and today marks a shift towards that accountability,” Kish said.

entries.title: Newsom Orders California to Accelerate AI Oversight Standards
entries.summary: The state will explore a slate of possible AI developer regulations, including a potential “kill switch” to shut down rogue models.
entries.content:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order Friday to accelerate state oversight of AI, exploring emergency “kill switches” for models and challenging President Donald Trump's hands-off approach amid rising industry safety fears.

The move follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “pace the frontier” of AI development so safety measures can catch up as well as warnings from researchers that companies are losing control of increasingly powerful systems that could “kill all humans” in the coming years.

“The fact that these labs are directly issuing urgent warnings about the risks of AI should be deeply concerning to everyone.” Newsom said on X. “And while Trump sits by and does nothing, California is signing nation-leading laws to provide the accountability this moment demands.”

The executive order seeks to “dramatically accelerate” state oversight of safety and security risks in AI systems by tasking a group of industry experts to build a safety plan for the state within 60 days.

Newsom asked the task force to explore the possibility of requiring third-party watchdogs to develop safety plans for leading AI companies. The order paves the way for California to force companies to develop a kill switch that could shut down frontier models in case of a security failure.

In his signature fashion, Newsom delivered the announcement alongside accusations that Trump is asleep at the wheel, adding that Washington has abdicated its responsibility to protect Americans.

Trump made his position clear on Monday when he asserted that his presidency is the only guardrail needed for AI. In a post from his Truth Social account, he called alarm bells from industry leaders “a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers,” adding, “The only one that is happy about it is China.”

The governor has leaned into his confrontations with Trump over the past few years, often using their bouts to elevate his national profile and position himself as a leading Democratic foil as he weighs a potential run for president.

This week, the AI debate has shaped the 2028 Democratic field as potential contenders scramble to carve out their own lanes on the issue.

On Friday, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order to increase oversight over the state’s data centers. And fellow Democratic governors have recently followed suit: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapirocalled for strict federal safeguards while Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is eyeing more regulation. Others have turned to Congress, like former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who claimed lawmakers have been sitting on their hands, and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who issued a public plea on Friday for more action from D.C.

Newsom signed a separate law Thursday forcing advertisers to disclose the use of AI-generated actors and recently approved rules requiring developers to report serious incidents.

The California governor faces a Sept. 30 deadline to sign a massive package of 20 strict AI regulations, including measures prohibiting automated hiring and firing decisions, curbing surveillance tools and regulating mass AI-driven layoffs.

entries.title: DCA, Dulles and BWI All Rank Below Average in Customer Survey
entries.summary: The D.C. area’s three major airports fared poorly in customer satisfaction scores.
entries.content:
Don’t expect to see a lot of happy faces in a D.C.-area airport.

The region’s three airports each ranked below average in a new customer satisfaction survey from analytics company J.D. Power. The list is based on responses from nearly 25,000 travelers to questions about “wayfinding,” terminal facilities, airport staff and retail shops.

Airports are ranked among others of a similar size. All three in the D.C.-area were considered in the “large” category with 10 to 32.9 million annual passengers.

Locally, Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport had the best ranking, though it still came in the bottom third of the list, taking spot 18 out of 24 for large airports. Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport came in right behind that in slot 19, and Washington Dulles International Airport ranked the worst of the local options at 21 on the list.

DCA and BWI both recently completed renovation projects. Dulles is up next, with a $22.5 billion makeover spearheaded by President Donald Trump slated to begin next year.

When the project was announced, Trump called Dulles “one of the worst airports anywhere in the world” and said neither Republicans or Democrats want to “be subject to this airport because this airport is a terrible place to be.”

Reagan National Airport is still dealing with the aftermath of a fatal 2025 collision that killed 67 people and drew attention to high-density flight traffic. The runway is one of the busiest in the nation. Virginia’s senators introduced a bill to Congress proposing limiting flights at the airport to improve safety.

entries.title: Pentagon Issues Male-Only Testosterone Guidance After Scrapping Its First Version
entries.summary: The new guideline does not include automatic blood testing for men 30 and older.
entries.content:
The Pentagon issued new, narrower testosterone-screening guidance for male troops Thursday, two weeks after abruptly pulling its first version.

The Defense Health Agency guideline leaves female service members out for now and makes clear that men 30 and older will not automatically receive a testosterone blood test. Instead, the Pentagon is requiring a symptom and risk-factor screening, with laboratory testing used to determine whether troops have a deficiency.

Men under 30 can also be screened if they request it or if a clinician sees a reason to evaluate them.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s original announcement did not distinguish between male and female troops. The Pentagon says separate guidance for female service members is still under review.

That is a notable change from the guidance the Pentagon published earlier this month and removed the next day. That version included separate pathways for men and women and called for mandatory testosterone blood tests for men 30 and older. The female pathway covered hormonal issues, low energy availability and menstrual problems.

The Pentagon said at the time that it had temporarily rescinded the document to make updates. Tim Parlatore, a senior adviser to Hegseth, later said the guidance had been posted “inadvertently” and needed more input to make sure it reflected current medical science.

Under the replacement, men 30 and older will first receive a structured assessment of symptoms and risk factors. A diagnosis requires symptoms consistent with low testosterone and low hormone levels measured on two separate days.

The guidance also tells clinicians to account for factors such as illness, severe sleep deprivation and extreme physical stress, which can temporarily lower testosterone levels.

Hegseth ordered the department in July to make testosterone screening mandatory during periodic health assessments for active-duty and reserve service members 30 and older, casting the effort as part of a broader push to improve health and military readiness.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Thursday that identifying and treating “suboptimal hormone levels” would help strengthen troops’ performance and maximize military readiness.

But the program drew questions from doctors and lawmakers over whether the Pentagon had shown a medical need to screen such a large population.

The Endocrine Society recommends against routine testosterone screening for men in the general population and says a diagnosis should be based on symptoms and repeatedly low testosterone levels.

A group of Senate Democrats also pressed Hegseth in July for the scientific basis of the policy, its cost, the testing protocols and evidence that screening or treatment would improve military readiness.

entries.title: Nationals Sign Ace Cade Cavalli to a Four-Year Contract Extension
entries.summary: The deal, which could be worth up to $70 million, also includes a club option for the 2031 season.
entries.content:
ST. LOUIS — The Nationals and Cade Cavalli have agreed to a four-year extension, the team announced Friday.

Cavalli will make $47 million over those years, according to a person familiar with the terms, though the deal also includes a club option for the 2031 season. If that option is eventually exercised, the contract could be worth up to $70 million, according to that person. That means Cavalli could be atop the Nats' rotation for the next half decade.

The right-hander, a first-round pick for the Nationals in 2020, has been one of the most consistent young starters in the league this season — and at times one of the most dominant. In 162 ⅔ innings, he has a 3.12 ERA. Since the start of August, he has a 2.06 ERA in eight starts, including an eight-inning, 10-strikeout gem against the Cubs on Aug. 13. The next outing, facing the Rangers, Cavalli, 28, struck out 11 in six innings.

Those were flashes of a shut-down ace. They also help explain why the Nationals wanted to extend him now, more than three years before he would have hit the free-agent market. The deal buys out Cavalli's last three years of arbitration eligibility, then will keep him in Washington for at least one more season. The Athletic first reported the figures of the extension.

And beyond extending a promising young pitcher, the deal is a step forward for the Nationals, who have often struggled to retain homegrown talent. They are, of course, now run by Paul Toboni, who is finishing his first season as the team's president of baseball operations. This is the first extension brokered by Toboni and his front office.

Cavalli starts against the Cardinals for the Nationals in St. Louis on Friday night.

entries.title: Judge Rules the EPA Illegally Terminated a $7 Billion Solar Program
entries.summary: The program was intended to make solar power accessible to lower-income Americans.
entries.content:
By Jennifer McDermott

The Trump administration illegally terminated a $7 billion Solar for All program intended to make solar power accessible to more than 900,000 lower-income Americans, a federal judge in Rhode Island ruled Friday.

The Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the Solar for All funds in August 2025 after President Donald Trump’s massive tax and spending law passed in Congress a month earlier, with Administrator Lee Zeldin calling the Biden-era grant program a “boondoggle.”

District Judge Mary McElroy wrote in the ruling that Congress clearly intended the EPA to continue administering the Solar for All grants that were already obligated. The EPA acted contrary to this intent and without any other statutory authority when it terminated the program, McElroy wrote. She vacated the termination.

The EPA said Friday it is reviewing the decision and considering options for appeal.

The lawsuit filed in Rhode Island by the Rhode Island AFL-CIO labor organization and others — including the public interest law center Rhode Island Center for Justice and the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors — highlighted the importance of the program for local workforces and lower-income communities seeking access to clean-energy project funding.

Patrick Crowley, president of the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, called the decision “a big victory” for states across the country.

“If and when the program does get up and running, there will be thousands and thousands of union jobs created across the United States,” he said Friday. “We were proud to be the lead plaintiff.”

Clean, affordable power like solar shouldn’t be a luxury, said Alex St. Pierre, vice president for environmental justice at Conservation Law Foundation, one of the nonprofit legal advocacy groups representing the plaintiffs.

“Communities have waited long enough,” St. Pierre said in a statement. "Nearly every family is looking for ways to cut their energy bill. These dollars should go where Congress intended: toward lower energy bills, less climate pollution, good jobs and cleaner air.”

In May, for the first time, solar supplied more of the nation’s electricity than coal.

The Trump administration has targeted a host of programs and policies dedicated to clean energy. The $7 billion Solar for All program was part of the $27 billion “green bank,” formally known as the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. It was established in the Democratic-backed climate law passed in 2022 under former President Joe Biden. The attorneys general of more than a dozen states also sued over the canceled solar program funding. A federal judge in Washington dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction in June. The plaintiffs have appealed.

The other $20 billion, also canceled by the Trump administration, was slated for eight community development banks and nonprofit organizations for tens of thousands of projects to combat the effects of climate change, such as residential energy efficiency projects to larger-scale investments such as community cooling. A divided federal appeals court said last month that the Trump administration improperly terminated the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, handing a win to a coalition of nonprofits picked to run the effort.

entries.title: Pentagon Failed to Disclose at Least Four Service Members Deaths: Report
entries.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the report “DISGUSTING and FAKE.”
entries.content:
The Pentagon has not disclosed the deaths of at least four additional service members who have died in the Middle East amid the ongoing military operations in Iran, The Washington Post reported Friday.

The Defense Department has faced questions about its transparency regarding the number of military fatalities and injuries that have been released regarding the war in Iran, which has lasted for nearly seven months with no clear end in sight. In July, The New York Times reported that the Pentagon did not disclose an episode of three Iranian strikes in Jordan that injured dozens of service members.

Details remain unclear on the four additional deaths that have not been disclosed, including when and how they died, officials told the Post, which said it granted the officials anonymity to discuss the matter. One official told the outlet that not all of the deaths are directly related to the Iran war but have involved American personnel who were present in the Middle East during hostilities.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dismissed the Post’s report.

“This is DISGUSTING and FAKE,” he wrote on X. “Shame on the Washington Post — they’re worse than Iranian state media.”

The Pentagon’s casualty database says at least 18 American service members have died and more than 400 troops have been injured in the Middle East since the U.S. and Israel began strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. The Pentagon classified four of the 18 deaths as “Overseas Operation” given that they occurred after the Trump administration reached a ceasefire deal with Iran.

The ceasefire has since collapsed due to ongoing violence in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Pentagon also has been slow to acknowledge destruction of military infrastructure caused by Iranian attacks. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told The Epoch Times earlier this month that the Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain sustained extensive damage following repeated Iranian attacks since February, despite the Pentagon initially saying these strikes have not significantly disrupted operations.

This article has been updated with a post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

entries.title: Trump Administration Clears Saudi F-35s Sale Despite Intelligence Warnings
entries.summary: U.S. intelligence has warned the sale could make the sensitive military technology accessible to China, which has military ties to the Saudis.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has formally cleared a potential $24.3 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, moving ahead despite U.S. intelligence warnings that China could gain access to some of the military’s most sensitive technology.

The State Department notified Congress on Thursday of the proposed sale of 48 F-35s, opening a 30-day congressional review period. The package also includes 49 Pratt & Whitney engines, secure communications equipment, electronic warfare support, training and other services.

The move comes after U.S. intelligence officials raised concerns that Saudi Arabia’s growing military and technology ties with China could create opportunities for Beijing to obtain information about the advanced fighter jet.

A recent U.S. intelligence assessment warned about Chinese military access to Saudi bases and Chinese technology in the kingdom’s telecommunications infrastructure, according to The New York Times. The assessment raised questions about whether sensitive F-35 systems could be adequately protected if the aircraft are based in Saudi Arabia.

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a senior Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said Thursday that the sale should not go forward “when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party.”

Congress is also investigating a separate incident involving sensitive F-35 technology and China after parts being shipped from Australia to the U.S. for repairs were diverted to Hong Kong this summer. Some of the components remain missing.

The State Department says the sale would strengthen Saudi homeland defense, improve interoperability with U.S., regional and NATO forces, and help Riyadh deter threats. It also says the deal “will not alter the military balance in the region.”

That assertion could draw scrutiny because Israel is the only country in the Middle East operating the F-35. If the sale is completed, Saudi Arabia would become the second — and the first Arab country — to fly the fifth-generation stealth fighter.

U.S. law requires the government to consider Israel’s qualitative military edge when approving major weapons sales to other countries in the region.

The State Department also says the sale would not hurt U.S. military readiness or require additional permanent U.S. personnel in Saudi Arabia.

President Donald Trump first publicly announced plans to sell F-35s to Saudi Arabia in November, ahead of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Washington. The White House later said Trump had approved a broader defense package that included future F-35 deliveries.

The formal notification brings the deal much closer to completion but does not make the sale final. Congress now has 30 calendar days to review the proposal and can try to block it through a joint resolution of disapproval.

Congressional opposition to Saudi weapons sales is not new, but the F-35 deal raises a different set of concerns because of the sensitivity of the aircraft’s technology.

The potential sale also comes as Saudi Arabia faces growing security threats from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Fighting between Saudi-backed forces and the Houthis has intensified, and Saudi territory has come under drone and missile attacks.

Lockheed Martin and Pratt & Whitney would be the main contractors for the jets and engines, respectively.

entries.title: Trump Says He Will Ban Three Major Media Outlets From the White House
entries.summary: The president later said the ban stemmed from “cumulative stories" reporters have written over that “purposefully" contain negative news about the administration.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced he will immediately ban media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, accusing the organizations of publishing “constant” false reports.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States,” he wrote Friday afternoon on Truth Social. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Trump’s post did not include additional details. When reporters later asked about how the ban would work in practice, the president said it would be “a very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here.”

Trump said the ban had stemmed from “just cumulative stories over the last few years” in which reporters “purposefully write negative news” about the administration.

“You need a free press, you need a fair press and an honest press,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office an hour after his initial announcement.

The president also suggested he could ban other outlets, including The New York Times and The Washington Post, which he said will "probably not" be on display anymore in the White House.

The White House referred The Washington Sun to Trump's comments in the Oval Office when asked for additional details.

"CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the outlet said in a statement. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right."

Trump has had a contentious history with prohibiting media access to his administration, issuing wide orders and subpoenas to individual reporters that have resulted in multiple legal challenges over the last two years. The White House barred reporters from unescorted access to the West Wing press office last year and revoked The Associated Press from covering presidential events, an order that was reversed when the outlet challenged the decision in federal court.

The Pentagon in June deemed its press office a “classified space” to restrict journalist access, following a 2025 crackdown on defense reporters meant to curb leaks, after which many turned in their press credentials in protest.

In his Truth Social post, the president characterized Politico as the recipient “of an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription” that he deemed “corruption.” In February 2025, the White House canceled $8 million in Politico subscriptions and products paid for across multiple federal agencies, saying the move was part of a wider effort to stop wasteful government spending.

The president’s announcement came two days after Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-North Carolina) said some members of Congress want to bar reporters from the Speaker’s Lobby, a crucial area off the House floor for journalists to question lawmakers.

entries.title: Vance Says Voters Can't Trust 'Crazy' Democrats to Fix the Country
entries.summary: The vice president spoke in Iowa in support of Republican candidates.
entries.content:
By Josh Boak and Seung Min Kim

COUNCIL BLUFFS, Iowa — Vice President JD Vance on Friday mounted a vigorous defense of the Trump administration's policies and Iowa GOP candidates on the November ballot, arguing that the Democrats had turned into the party of “lunatics," in his second trip to the politically consequential state this year.

While in Iowa, Vance tried to nationalize the elections, invoking Democratic candidates in other states such as Kansas, Texas and New York at a time when the state's Democratic ticket has tried to keep its focus local. But he took plenty of swings at Iowa Democrats, saying their candidate for governor, Rob Sand, was a “career politician" and not a moderate, despite his public persona.

“Let's send the crazy packing and get them out of Washington, D.C., and get them out of Des Moines,” Vance told the crowd at the Mid-America Center in Council Bluffs, located on the western edge of the once-Republican stronghold state. Iowa has found itself with competitive races for the Senate and the governor’s mansion this year.

Zach Lahn, the GOP nominee for governor, campaigned alongside Vance, who showered him with effusive praise. But missing was Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, the party’s Senate candidate, who did not attend the rally Friday due to previously scheduled events, according to her campaign.

Council Bluffs is home to Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for the Senate who represents the area in the Statehouse.

“It’s no mystery why Vance is here,” Turek wrote in a fundraising appeal ahead of Vance’s visit. “It’s because his billionaire bosses are terrified that their grip over Iowa is slipping — and with it, their narrow Senate majority.”

Vance spoke about job growth under the Trump administration and was greeted with cheers for the administration’s work on immigration and border security. Continuing on his laundry list of White House accomplishments, Vance mentioned the administration’s work to get “most favored nation” prescription drug prices and highlighted the policies on not taxing tips or overtime and protecting Social Security.

In the agriculture-heavy state, Vance said he was perhaps “most proud of what we’ve been able to do for Iowa farmers,” pointing to efforts by the administration to open up more global markets to American-grown food.

Still, Vance urged voters to be patient.

“Whenever you hear me talk during this midterm campaign, I’ll say Rome was not built in a day because we know there’s a lot of work to do,” Vance said.

Vance took his first trip to the state as vice president in May, campaigning alongside Rep. Zach Nunn, one of the party’s most endangered incumbents this year. Nunn and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, another Iowa Republican, voted earlier this week in a symbolic measure to halt the war in Iran, underscoring how the military conflict that Trump launched is causing political troubles for his own party.

The vice president has been one of the most visible surrogates on the midterm campaign trail, jetting to locations such as Kansas, Wisconsin and his native Ohio to promote Republican candidates and the administration’s achievements.

Friday’s rally location is in Iowa’s 4th Congressional District, which is being vacated by Republican Rep. Randy Feenstra after his failed bid for governor. Democrat Dave Dawson and Republican Chris McGowan are vying for the seat. That race is not considered one of the more competitive races in this election.

Vance’s visit to the state shows Republican candidates are in political trouble in November, said Katie Smith, a spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, in a statement.

“Iowans have had enough of their D.C.-first, Iowa-last priorities and will hold them all accountable for their agenda that’s caused skyrocketing prices at the pump, grocery stores, and doctor’s office,” Smith said.

___
Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut contributed to this report from Des Moines, Iowa.

entries.title: Montgomery County Police Chief Abruptly Resigns
entries.summary: Marc Yamada had served the police department for nearly 40 years.
entries.content:
Montgomery County Police Chief Marc Yamada is stepping down from his position effective immediately, marking an abrupt end to the role he’s held for the past two years.

County Executive Marc Elrich announced Yamada’s resignation in a statement Friday, thanking him for nearly four decades of service to the Montgomery County Police Department. He did not say why Yamada is resigning.

Yamada could not be immediately reached for comment.

The sudden resignation came just before the Montgomery County inspector general released an investigation into alleged misconduct by a Montgomery County Police Department executive. They did not name the executive, but whistleblowers had previously filed complaints about Yamada’s use of funds on a trip to Las Vegas.

The report concluded the executive had been absent from work for at least five days to attend an out-of-state conference in June 2026 without taking leave or adjusting their schedule to make up the time.

Investigators found the executive had invited a relative also employed by the county to a conference along with several other high-ranking MCPD employees, where they attended a golf tournament. The executive also admitted to drinking two alcoholic beverages during the tournament, the report states.

Photographs posted on the event’s website show the executive in civilian clothing and apparently unarmed, according to the report.

Inspector General Megan Davey Limarzi recommended the county determine whether to recover the executive's 40 hours of pay, clarify time and attendance expectations, update its policy to require all supervisors to review and approve timecards and implement a policy clarifying when employees may attend social events during work hours.

Elrich said he had selected Assistant Chief Darren Franke to serve as the MCPD’s acting chief of police until a permanent replacement is appointed.

The police department released a statement following Elrich’s announcement saying it received notification that Yamada had resigned.

“During this leadership transition, the department will continue its day-to-day operations and remain focused on serving Montgomery County,” the statement read. “We also remain committed to transparency, accountability and maintaining the public’s trust as we move forward.”

Yamada was appointed in May 2024, becoming the county’s 18th police chief. The department, with roughly 1,100 personnel, serves more than 1 million residents across a 507-square-mile jurisdiction.

This article has been updated with details from a Montgomery County inspector general report.

entries.title: D.C. Preservation Official Says Trump Needs to Scrap His Arch for a Smaller Monument
entries.summary: Administration officials have been citing a plan from 1925 that authorized two pillars as justification for his 250-foot arch.
entries.content:
Local preservationists are pushing back against President Donald Trump’s plan to construct a massive triumphal arch and asking him instead to consider building slender columns to protect the capital’s visual harmony.

Trump officials have repeatedly cited a 1925 Congress-approved plan to erect the pillars as justification for his proposed 250-foot arch at Memorial Circle, outside of Arlington National Cemetery. In a letter on Wednesday, Andrew Lewis, an official in D.C.’s Historic Preservation Office, called Trump’s plan “antithetical” to the 1925 design proposal and said the arch would limit the historic view corridor.

If a monument project must proceed, Lewis said, it should be the two columns proposed a century ago, rather than Trump’s massive arch, to maintain visual unity.

“The proposed Triumphal Arch would effectively replace much of the important view with a frame — a massive frame that would significantly narrow and restrict, if not completely obstruct portions of the view corridor,” said the letter, first reported by The Washington Post on Friday.

The administration has consulted D.C. and Virginia’s preservation offices as part of a required federal review.

Officials with the National Park Service previously said construction of the arch would negatively impact dozens of historic sites in the area, including the Arlington Memorial Bridge, the Lincoln Memorial and the National Mall. Earlier this week, the agency sent a letter to the local historic preservation offices saying that despite the arch’s projected visual consequences, construction should proceed as planned.

In his letter, Lewis said the Park Service lacks a complete understanding of how the arch will affect nearby areas and disputed the Park Service’s assertion that the arch’s significance is “location dependent.”

“The language used to describe the nature of the adverse effects significantly underestimates the degree to which the integrity of the affected historic properties would be diminished,” the letter said. “For example, the arch would not merely be ‘prominently visible.’ Instead, it would visually overwhelm the surrounding historic context.”

The two-column monument approved in 1925 would have accentuated the existing views and monuments at the time, including the Lincoln Memorial. Approved decades after Reconstruction, they also aimed to represent the country’s reunification, with one pillar representing the North and the other the South — an intention Lewis said Trump’s proposed arch does not meet.

Officials with a nonprofit historic preservation group sent their own letter to the Park Service on Wednesday: Judy Chesser and Paul Edmondson, officials with Committee of 100 on the Federal City, said the agency is failing to meet its legal obligations to consider alternative structures and locations for the project.

An Interior Department spokesperson said it has followed all laws and has received robust public feedback, with over 100,000 responses.

“To infer this process is unlawful shows a lack of understanding of the facts,” the spokesperson said in a statement to The Washington Sun.

Lewis said despite mounting negative feedback, the Park Service doesn’t seem to be adequately acknowledging “fervent opposition” expressed by the majority of the public. A recent Historic Preservation Office review showed opposition to the arch has been expressed by residents of all 50 states and most U.S. territories, according to Lewis’ letter. Locally, 93% of the 11,000 comments from D.C. residents strongly oppose the arch.

A federal commission stacked with Trump allies has already approved the arch plan. A second commission still has to give final approval, though the construction process itself has already prompted an escalating legal battle.

entries.title: DOJ Can’t Convince a Judge That ‘Anti-Weaponization’ Payments Are Dead
entries.summary: “The issues that underlie this case are still alive and kicking, in my view,” the judge said.
entries.content:
A federal judge aired doubts Friday that President Donald Trump’s $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund is as dead as the Justice Department has insisted it is.

“The issues that underlie this case are still alive and kicking, in my view,” U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Virginia said at a hearing.

Brinkema seemed skeptical of the government’s bid to throw out a lawsuit challenging the fund and a related tax-immunity deal for Trump and his family on the grounds that the case is moot.

The judge didn’t rule on the government’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit, saying an order could come in the near future. But she indicated she wasn’t convinced that administration officials had fully abandoned the fund — or, at least the idea of steering taxpayer money to people claiming to have been unfairly targeted by federal authorities.

The Justice Department created the fund in May under a highly unusual settlement in a separate case in Florida between Trump, the DOJ and the IRS over the leak of Trump’s tax returns years earlier. The federal judge in the Florida case recently rebuked the agreement as the product of collusion among the parties and manipulation of the legal process to benefit Trump and his allies.

The fund was designed to compensate people who claimed they were wrongfully investigated or prosecuted, a group that lawmakers and legal advocates argued could include people who participated in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot. The immunity deal also purported to insulate Trump, his family and businesses from tax liabilities.

Attorney General Todd Blanche repeatedly said the fund was not moving forward following rulings from multiple judges against blocking the settlement, at least temporarily, and after scrutiny from Democrats and Republicans in Congress.

“It’s dead,” Blanche told lawmakers at his Senate confirmation hearing in July. He followed up with a two-page order in August claiming to rescind the fund and modify the agreement.

In court Friday, Brinkema said she was satisfied that the fund itself “now is gone” after hearing Blanche’s congressional testimony. But she questioned, as she has throughout the litigation, whether the Trump administration could create a “functional equivalent” of the fund through another mechanism.

She zeroed in on the possibility that the administration could use the federal Judgment Fund, which pays court judgments and settlements against the government, to compensate people the administration favors.

She appeared to allude to a recent payout the Justice Department made to an anti-abortion activist who was convicted during the Biden administration of blocking access to an abortion clinic. The activist, Paul Vaughn, received a seven-figure settlement in July. He had been pardoned by Trump while his case was on appeal.

“This concept of taxpayer money being used to promote particular political viewpoints,” the judge said, “that’s the gravamen, as I understand it.”

She also said administration officials had contradicted Blanche’s assurances that the fund was not proceeding. Trump has said he wished the fund could continue, and Blanche has defended the underlying idea of redressing what he called “victims of a Department of Justice that was absolutely weaponized.”

At one point, Brinkema balked at a suggestion by DOJ attorney Andrew Block that there was no remedy for the plaintiffs to seek in the case. Brinkema floated the idea of requiring a “neutral” official, outside the Justice Department, to oversee the Judgment Fund and ensure payouts are handled properly.

But she said the litigation was nowhere near that stage.

Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy group, filed the lawsuit challenging the fund in May. The plaintiffs include a former federal prosecutor who handled several Jan. 6 cases.

Two rulings by Brinkema over the summer blocked the Trump administration from implementing the fund while the litigation proceeds.

Democracy Forward later added new plaintiffs and allegations to the case calling the tax-immunity deal unlawful. They argue the deal will put IRS employees in an “untenable position by compelling them to carry out unlawful orders” to terminate tax audits. Part of Friday’s hearing involved whether IRS employees from the Treasury Department’s union have the legal right to join the lawsuit.

In their motion to dismiss, DOJ lawyers said the lawsuit isn’t viable because it targets an anti-weaponization fund that “has never existed and will not exist.”

They also argued that the plaintiffs did not have legal standing to challenge Trump’s immunity deal, which the DOJ described as a “third-party settlement agreement to a civil action in another district with which they have a policy disagreement.”

“The Justice Department and Attorney General have now said countless times, in public, to this Court in briefs, and to Congress in sworn testimony, that the idea of the Anti-Weaponization Fund at the heart of this case is dead and will not go forward,” they wrote. “The time has come to stop this inquisition.”

entries.title: Trump Defends Bid to Put His Name on the Kennedy Center
entries.summary: Trump did not directly say whether he planned to demolish the theater, as he's threatened to do, but called the building “a dump” on Friday.
entries.content:
By Jonathan J. Cooper

President Donald Trump on Friday defended his push to put his name on the Kennedy Center, saying he deserves to be recognized for trying to save Washington's premier performing arts venue after his takeover was blamed for triggering its financial distress.

Trump did not directly respond when a reporter asked whether he planned to demolish the theater, as he's threatened to do, but said “the place is a dump” and he would “do a better job building it than anybody else.”

He said the Kennedy Center would require an ongoing subsidy to stay open and suggested it would be his burden to raise money to fill that gap.

“Why should I do everything and then for the rest of my life, have to go out and raise money?” Trump said.

He said only he could have secured the $257 million that Congress has approved for Kennedy Center repairs.

“I think the Trump administration should be recognized as having saved the Kennedy Center because nobody else could do it,” he added, repeating a comment he made days earlier while campaigning in North Carolina.

The Kennedy Center board, which is aligned with the president, voted Tuesday to close the center indefinitely for repairs hours after a judge blocked their plans to return Trump's name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it.

Trump on Friday called U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper “a very hostile judge."

He spoke in the Oval Office during a health care event as his Health and Human Services Secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., looked on. The venue was designated by Congress as a memorial for the secretary's uncle, President John F. Kennedy.

“I should be very careful because Bobby is standing right behind me," Trump said. “And I cherish that, too. I actually like the name of Kennedy and Trump, Trump and Kennedy, because it showed bipartisanship. It showed a Republican Party and a Democrat party working together.”

A wave of artists have canceled their Kennedy Center appearances in that past year after the Trump-loyal board added his name to the building's facade, renaming it The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts.

Cooper ruled that Trump's name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

entries.title: Trump Says U.S. Will Have ‘Permanent Control’ Over Military Presence In Greenland
entries.summary: The agreement means “no U.S. adversary” could ever have a military base or make “sensitive investments” in the territory without approval, Trump said.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said the United States has entered into an agreement with the kingdom of Denmark that would give America “permanent control over security, and all other needs” related to the territory of Greenland.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Friday afternoon.

The two countries were closing in on a deal earlier Friday to increase U.S. military presence on the island, Reuters reported. Trump said the agreement means “no U.S. adversary” could ever generate a military presence or make “sensitive investments” in the territory without approval.

The president has insisted the U.S. take control of the strategic Arctic island in large part to gain access to its key mineral resources and military positioning.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration held talks over the fate of the autonomous Danish territory that ended in a “fundamental disagreement” with Danish representatives — with foreign officials repeatedly asserting that Greenland is “not for sale” — though negotiations resumed this month in a more positive direction.

The three governments are expected to sign the agreement next week at the U.N. General Assembly in New York City, according to a press statement from the office of Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.

The deal must still be approved by Greenland’s parliament before going into effect, the release said.

"The agreement recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all," Nielsen said.
